However, we want to find the real part of the with the maximum imaginary part. This Z would lie directly above the center of the circle, and thus the real part would be the same as the x-value of the center of the circle. So all we have to do is find this value and we’re done.

Solution 6 (Euclidean geometry and coordinates)[edit]

If you've read Evan Chen's book EGMO (Euclidean Geometry in Mathematical Olympiads), you know that is a real number is just a fancy way of saying that are points on a cyclic quadrilateral. The proof of this can be found in EGMO or other sources, and this is the key to the problem.

And the three given points already define the circle that circumscribes that cyclic quadrilateral. So all we need to do is get the equation for that circle in the Cartesian plane, and then maximize the y-coordinate of .

To find the center of the circumcircle, find the intersection of the perpendicular bisectors. One of them is just , and the second is . So we have the point (56, 61) as the center of the circle. The distance from this point to all three points is . The square of the radius of this circle is . So the equation for the circle is . To maximize the y-coordinate, which does not have to be a positive integer, but does (per AIME rules given it's the answer), by the trivial inequality , so is the answer.
